      BRIEF OF KEN PAXTON, ATTORNEY GENERAL OF TEXAS AS AMICI CURIAE
           IN SUPPORT OF AMERICAN STEWARDS OF LIBERTY, INC.’S
                  MOTION TO DEFER DETERMINATION OF NEED

    The Attorney General (AG), in representing the interests of the citizens of Texas, respectfully

submits this Amicus Brief in support of abating any decision in furtherance of the Permian Basin

Reliability Plan (Plan). Any further action should be deferred until the 90th Legislature is given

time to consider the immense impact on the citizens of Texas and is able to provide clear policy

guidance to the Public Utility Commission (PUC). The AG does not seek or request intervention,

only to express grave concerns with this process and to ensure that any decision is in the best

interest of the citizens of Texas.

    I.      Introduction

    H.B. 5066 (88(R)) amended sections 39.166 and 39.167 of the Texas Utilities Code (PURA),

directing the Commission to develop reliability plans for areas of “rapid electrical load growth”

and the Permian Basin. Act of May 28, 2023, 88th Leg., R.S., ch. 892, 2023 Tex. Gen. Laws 2640

(codified at Tex. Util. Code §§ 37.056, 37.0561, and 39.167(expired Sept. 1, 2025)); Tex. Util.

Code §§ 39.166; 39.137. The Commission implemented the requirements of H.B. 5066 by

formulating and approving the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (Plan). PUC Control No. 55718,

Item 52. H.B. 5066 makes no mention of extra high voltage 765-kilovolt lines (765KV), nor was

it the apparent intent of the Legislature to have these transmission lines included under the Plan

when the bill was enrolled. Thus, the Commission has created a Plan that appears to exceed the

original intent of H.B. 5066 such that the Commission is no longer aligned with the expectations

of the Legislature. All further consideration of implementing the Plan should be paused until the

Legislature has time to review the impact of the enormous policy decision envisioned in adding

765KV lines to the state’s transmission system.




                                             Page 3
     II.      The Plan appears to go further than the directions provided by the Legislature

          Administrative agencies have only those powers expressly conferred and those necessary

to accomplish their duties. State v. Jackson, 376 S.W.2d 341, 344 (Tex.1964); Sexton v. Mount

Olivet Cemetery Ass'n, 720 S.W.2d 129, 137 (Tex. App.—Austin 1986, writ ref'd n.r.e.). The

Legislature of Texas sets policy through the enactment of laws and the Commission, as a creature

of statute, is tasked with implementing those laws. Here, the Commission has approved a Plan that

appears to reach beyond the Legislature’s clear direction. The Legislature must be afforded the

time to review the Plan and its potential impacts so it can then enact additional legislation to

provide whatever additional guidance it deems fit. As the Legislature is already endeavoring to

tackle the growth in electric demand spurred by data centers popping up across the state, now is

the ideal time for the Legislature to review the Plan as part of a holistic review of the state’s

reliability efforts.

          As a state agency, the Commission must operate within the bounds of its enabling statutes.

The Legislature directed the Commission to develop a plan, not to implement it in the manner it

plans. When one is granted an apple, he does not acquire the whole tree. That is even more true

here when that Plan contemplates the use of 765 KV transmission lines which do not appear to

have been contemplated by the legislature. A statute grants an agency exclusive jurisdiction when

its “language clearly expresses the Legislature's intent for the [agency] to have exclusive

jurisdiction over matters the [statute] governs.” Subaru of America, Inc., v. David McDavid Nissan,

84 S.W.3d 212, 223 (Tex. 2002). The Legislature has given an agency exclusive jurisdiction over

a matter when the statute either (1) contains express language to that effect; or (2) creates “a

pervasive regulatory scheme indicat[ing] that the Legislature intended for the regulatory process

to be the exclusive means of remedying the problem” at hand. Oncor Electric Delivery Company




                                               Page 4
 LLC v. Chaparral Energy, LLC, 546 S.W.3d 133, 138 (Tex. 2018) (quoting In re Sw. Bell Tel. Co.,

235 S.W.3d 619, 624–625 (Tex. 2007)). Of course, “[i]n deciding whether a ‘pervasive regulatory

scheme’ exists, the statutory language is determinative.” Id. (citing In re Entergy, 142 S.W.3d 316,

322–323 (Tex. 2004)). PURA Sections 11.002, 11.008, 14.001, and 31.001(a) all indicate the

Legislature's creation of a pervasive regulatory scheme. See id. at 138. Tex. Util. Code §§ 11.002

(establishing a comprehensive and adequate regulatory system for public utilities); 11.008

(allowing liberal construction of PURA to promote effectiveness and efficiency of the regulation

of public utilities); 14.001 (authorizing the Commission the general power to regulate and

supervise the business of each public utility within its jurisdiction, including anything specifically

designated or implied by PURA); 31.001(a) (protecting and ensuring public interest and protection

in rates and services of electrical utilities). PURA Sections 39.166 and 39.167 are also part of that

regulatory scheme and indicate the Legislature required the Commission to create a Plan. Tex. Util.

Code § 39.166; and Act of May 28, 2023, 88th Leg., R.S., ch. 892, 2023 Tex. Gen. Laws 2640.

While the Commission has been given exclusive jurisdiction and authority to formulate a Plan, it

is less clear the Legislature intended or authorized the Commission to construct a network of

765KV transmission lines.

   a. H.B. 5066 does not expressly authorize incorporating KV765 lines into the Plan.

   In interpreting sections 39.166 and 39.167, a court would consider the entire legislative

structure and context to reflect the legislature’s intent. Rodriquez v. Waak, 562 S.W.3d 570, 576

(Tex. App.—Houston [1st Dist.] 2018), aff’d, 603 S.W.3d 103 (Tex. 2020). “When construing a

statute, [the] primary objective is to determine the Legislature's intent which, when possible, we

discern from the plain meaning of the words chosen.” In re Estate of Nash, 220 S.W.3d 914, 917

(Tex. 2007); see also Tex. Gov't Code § 312.005.




                                              Page 5
     Both sections mandate the Commission to develop a reliability plan to implement, but nowhere

in the plain language of the statute are 765KV lines mentioned. Without that express mandate, the

Commission should pause to allow the Legislature time to evaluate the benefits and risks of these

massive transmission lines. While the potential benefit of such lines may be significant, so is the

risk of damage to privately owned lands and natural resources and the Legislature has not yet had

the ability to balance those interests.

        Neither H.B. 5066 as Introduced nor as Enrolled contains language that would lend

credence to the Commission’s interpretation that 765KV lines should be included as part of the

statutorily directed Plan. In fact, the specific language provides for the Plan to:

        (1) address extending transmission services where mineral resources have been found

        (2) address increasing available capacity to meet forecasted load; and

        (3) provide available infrastructure to reduce interconnection times in areas without access

        to transmission service.

Act of May 28, 2023, 88th Leg., R.S., ch. 892, 2023 Tex. Gen. Laws 2640 (codified at Tex. Util.

Code §§ 37.056, 37.0561, and 39.167(expired Sept. 1, 2025)). In the Commission's Order

approving the Plan, the Commission approved at least three 765KV lines, going further than

addressing localized need as it further plans to build the lines on a “statewide basis.” Order 55718.

Public sentiment is loud and clear; the public strongly opposes the Plan and its massive reach. The

purpose and spirit of H.B. 5066 is limited to improving and creating regional frameworks. And,

before the Commission uses that authority to revamp the state’s transmission network, the

Legislature must be allowed to review the potential impacts of a decision as monumental as adding

765KV lines and provide its guidance on whether and how to implement such a change.

    b. The Fiscal Note does not reflect the Commission’s expansive implementation.




                                               Page 6
    The Legislative Budget Board (LBB) must include in its fiscal note for a bill any provision that

would authorize or require expenditures outside of the General Appropriations Act. Tex. Govt

Code § 314.001. LBB must include a cost estimate for a five-year period that begins on the

effective date of the bill and must state whether costs or diversions will be involved after that

period. Id. § 314.002. LBB included no additional anticipated costs to the state or consumers in its

five-year forecast. Fiscal Note, H.B. 5066, 88th Leg., R.S. (2023). A comparison to another fiscal

note from the same session is instructive. S.B. 2012 (88R), as Introduced, had a fiscal note that

noted the bill would require transmission and distribution to build out generation capacity and that

such costs would be recovered in the utility rates. Fiscal Note, S.B. 2012, 88th Leg., R.S. (2023).

Clearly, when LBB anticipated future costs for building electric utility infrastructure during the

88th Session, it noted that there would be a cost and how the cost would be recovered. No such

language was included for H.B. 5066.

   In addition, a Fiscal Note must be attached to the bill for the remainder of its lifespan, including

as part of committee reports and all subsequent printings, including when it is submitted to the

Governor. Tex. Govt Code § 314.003. As previously established, LBB noted no anticipated cost

for this bill, even costs that would be recovered through utility rates. This means that neither the

members who reviewed the bill, nor the committees that considered the bill, nor any member who

voted to approve the bill, nor the Governor, had any notice of the immense costs that the Plan as

currently envisioned by PUC would incur.

   Under the Plan, the Commission is attempting to approve and build lines across the entire state

in an extraordinary change and increase of expense to the citizens of Texas without clear

Legislative direction. These costs should not be borne by the public unless such costs have been

clearly authorized by the Legislature. The Legislature should be allowed to review the proposed




                                              Page 7
 Plan’s costs and the fiscal impact to the state so that it can make an informed policy decision.

While the Legislature has begun to review the impact of data centers across the state, it should be

allowed to formulate the state’s overall policy going forward considering the enormous costs of

PUC’s proposed Plan.

    III.      No Bill Analysis Mentions 765KV Lines

    “Ordinarily, the truest manifestation of what legislators intended is what lawmakers enacted,

the literal text they voted on.” Alex Sheshunoff Mgmt. Servs., L.P. v. Johnson, 209 S.W.3d 644, 651

(Tex. 2006). H.B. 5066 was authored to address concerns “that the current process for building

electric transmission may not keep up with demand or allow adequate advanced planning for large

new loads.” House Research Organization, Bill Digest, Tex. H.B. 5066 (2nd Reading) & C.S.H.B.

5066, 88th R.S. (2023); accord, Senate Research Center, Business and Commerce Committee, Bill

Analysis, Tex. H.B. 5066, 88th R.S. (2023). This is especially true for areas of rapid growth in the

industrial sector, including where heavy oil and gas development are located. State Affairs

Committee Report (Substituted), Bill Analysis, Tex. C.S.H.B. 5066, 88th R.S. (2023).

    In general, the bill revises provisions under PURA relating to the criteria the Commission must

consider in granting or denying a certificate of convenience and necessity (CCN) for an electric

utility by, among other things, requiring the Commission to consider historical load, forecasted

load growth, and additional load currently seeking interconnection. The bill expedites the

processing of applications for CCNs for new transmission facilities by changing the general

deadline for the Commission to approve or deny an application to the 180th day after the filing

date. 1 Nowhere in any version of the bill are 765KV lines mentioned, and the Legislature had


1
  The bill summary provided by the legislature states: “House Bill 5066 amends the Utilities Code to require the
[Commission] to direct ERCOT to identify each region in which transmission capacity is insufficient to meet the
region's existing and forecasted electrical load and develop a reliability plan to serve existing and forecasted electrical
load in the identified region. The bill requires the Commission to develop a plan to implement each adopted reliability


                                                        Page 8
 notice of these lines and did not include them in the bill. Testimony heard on the bill in fact reveals

that legislators were specifically warned against the implementation of these lines without further

studies being done by the Commission.

    Generally, legislative history is not considered by a court unless the plain language is

ambiguous, and then a court will apply its words according to their normal meaning without resort

to rules of construction. See, e.g., In re Estate of Nash, 220 S.W.3d 914, 917 (Tex.2007). But where

the Commission has seemingly read words and requirements into the Plan in excess of the

legislative intent, legislative history can clarify that intent and clear the ambiguity. The history of

the bill shows that there was no contemplation of 765KV lines in the Plan, much less to the extent

that the Commission intends to implement and install across the entire state.

    The House Research Committee, in reviewing the bill, determined that the bill “would specify

that if the Commission identified a region in which transmission capacity was insufficient to meet

the region's existing and forecasted electrical load, [the Commission] would be required to develop

and implement a reliability plan to serve existing and forecasted electrical load in the identified

region.” House Research Organization, State Affairs Committee, Bill Analysis, Tex. H.B. 5066,

88th R.S. (2023). The Committee summarized both PURA sections 39.166 and 39.167 as requiring

“timely planning, identification, and approval of necessary transmission service improvements

under existing rules” and further that the bill would “amend the criteria considered by [the

Commission] when granting a certificate of public convenience and necessity to electric utilities

to include the need for extending transmission service where existing or projected electrical loads



plan to ensure timely development and approval of necessary transmission service improvements. Moreover, the bill
requires the Commission to direct ERCOT to develop a reliability plan for the Permian Basin region not later than
January 30, 2024.”
Texas Legislature Online, 89th Legislature Second Called Session, Text for 88(R) HB5066 by Geren, Enrolled Bill
Summary, https://capitol.texas.gov/BillLookup/BillSummary.aspx?LegSess=88R&Bill=HB5066 (last visited August
20, 2026.


                                                   Page 9
 would be underserved.” Id. Nowhere in this analysis nor in the bill is the adoption of new and

costly transmission lines mentioned.

   The intent of the bill is to “spur a bolder, more proactive approach that better syncs the

transmission planning and construction process with the dynamic needs of Texas customers by

requiring ERCOT, the Commission, and utilities to plan the grid more proactively based on the

information utilities have about growth load in their area.” Id. The Report also summarized the

difference between the introduced version of the bill and the Committee substitute, but nowhere

in that description are 765KV lines mentioned. In fact, no version of the bill through any stage

contemplates those lines.

   The Business and Commerce Committee Report from the Senate Research Center stated much

of the same as was observed in the House reports. In short, the intent of the author was summarized

as amending PURA to provide electricity service in areas of the state that lacked the necessary

transmission lines. Senate Research Center, Business and Commerce Committee, Bill Analysis,

Tex. C.S.H.B. 5066, 88th R.S. (2023). Again, there is nothing that makes mention of 765KV lines.

Of the many interim charges the Senate Committee on Business and Commerce was tasked with

ahead of the 89th Session, primary focus was given to the electrical grid in Texas. Senate

Committee on      Business    and   Commerce,     Interim   Report    to   the 89th   Legislature,

https://texashistory.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metapth1870648/ (last accessed August 20, 2026). Charge

No. 4 was to assess power transmission across the state. Id. To this charge, the Committee heard

testimony from the public and other stakeholders, including Commissioner Lore Cobos, stating

that the transmission infrastructure in Texas remains bottlenecked. Id. p. 13. Testimony included

ERCOT reporting that the demand for electricity in Texas would rise to around 150,000 megawatts

by 2030. Id. The forecasted load for the Permian Basin alone was estimated to be 43% higher than




                                            Page 10
 previously expected. Id. The testimony also showed that ERCOT has studied options for replacing

areas of 345KV lines with a 765KV “backbone.” Id. Testimony also covered the high energy

consumption and needs for cryptocurrency mining and AI data centers, part of the driving need for

more electricity demand. Id. at p. 14. Witness testimony also showed concerns over transparency

around transmission costs, currently comprising 30 to 40 percent of a customer’s electric bills,

further suggesting that legislative review is crucial to address rising costs and allocations. Id.

(citing Potomac Economics. 2023 State of the Market Report for the ERCOT Electricity Market,

22. (May 2024). https://www.potomaceconomics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/2023-State-

of-the-Market-Report_Final_060624.pdf.) The conclusion of the report included a direction to the

Commission that there should be an independent analysis of the direct and indirect costs associated

with the transition to 765KV lines. Senate Interim Report at p. 14.

   Under Charge 5, for managing the growth in Texas in relation to energy coverage, the

Committee heard further testimony from multiple witnesses regarding extra high-voltage

transmission lines to transport power more efficiently, e.g., 765KV lines, but the Committee

specifically cautioned against the quick adoption of these lines outside of the legislative process,

due to other significant investment and regulatory planning required. Id. The Committee stressed

the need to reevaluate the current process for apportioning transmission costs as the Legislature

considers new transmission infrastructure. Id.

   The Legislature had the opportunity to consider whether it wanted to include 765KV lines in

H.B. 5066 or any other bill during the 88th or 89th sessions but did not do so. In fact, the above

testimony, and further hearings discussed below, including the Committee’s own words, show that

the Legislature wants to consider the implementation of higher voltage lines, which would include

765KV lines. Yet while the Legislature has directed the Commission to approve and implement




                                             Page 11
 the Plan, it did so without the contemplation of including an authorization for 765V lines. If the

legislature wanted those lines, it would have said so.

    IV.      Testimony on Floor foreshadowing of what could happen has happened

    The House Committee on State Affairs, in addition to hearing live testimony on H.B. 5066, at

the same hearing also heard testimony on H.B. 4831. 2 A representative from both the Commission

and ERCOT appeared as resource witnesses. Representative Raymond wanted clarification on

what the assessments would include under the bill, to which the Commission responded that once

the details of the finalized plan are worked out, and once they get input from the Legislature, that

cost, and cost estimates are something that needs to be addressed. 5:00:47. In further clarification

to the representative, the Commission again stated that cost impact is something that has to be

addressed [by the Legislature]. 5:01:33.

    Testimony for H.B. 4831 clearly demonstrates that the Commission is aware that the

Legislature defines its limits through “guardrails” and the Legislature must provide it with the

“guardrails” because these are matters of policy. 5:03:27. Testimony from the Commission makes

clear that even the Commission understands there are limits to be observed, especially in the face

of policy questions. It is striking that, in contrast, for H.B. 5066, the Commission does not seek

guardrails or further policy instruction from the Legislature.

    V.       Conclusion

    The Commission should defer to the Legislature and abate any decisions regarding further

development, implementation, or approval of any transmission lines under the Plan. The

Legislature, as the policy-making body of this state, must have the opportunity to review the Plan

          IN SUPPORT OFAMERICAN STEWARDS OFLIBERTY, INC.'S
                MOTION TO DEFER DETERMINATION OF NEED

   The Attorney General (AG), in representing the interests of the citizens of Texas, respectfully

submits this Amicus Brief in support of abating any decision in furtherance of the Permian Basin

Reliability Plan (Plan). Any further action should be deferred until the 90th Legislature is given

time to consider the immense impact on the citizens of Texas and is able to provide clear policy

guidance to the Public Utility Commission (PUC). The AG does not seek or request intervention,

only to express grave concerns with this process and to ensure that any decision is in the best

interest ofthe citizens of Texas.

   I.      Introduction

   H.B. 5066 (88(R)) amended sections 39.166 and 39.167 ofthe Texas Utilities Code (PURA),

directing the Commission to develop reliability plans for areas of "rapid electrical load growth"

and the Permian Basin. Act ofMay 28,2023,88th Leg., R.S., ch. 892,2023 Tex. Gen. Laws 2640

(codified at Tex. Util. Code §§ 37.056, 37.0561, and 39.167(expired Sept. 1, 2025)); Tex. Util.

Code §§ 39.166; 39.137. The Commission implemented the requirements of H.B. 5066 by

formulating and approving the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (Plan). PUC Control No. 55718,

Item 52. H.B. 5066 makes no mention of extra high voltage 765-kilovolt lines (765KV), nor was

it the apparent intent of the Legislature to have these transmission lines included under the Plan

when the bill was enrolled. Thus, the Commission has created a Plan that appears to exceed the

original intent of H.B. 5066 such that the Commission is no longer aligned with the expectations

of the Legislature. All further consideration of implementing the Plan should be paused until the

Legislature has time to review the impact of the enormous policy decision envisioned in adding

765KV lines to the state's transmission system.

     II.      The Plan appears to go further than the directions provided by the Legislature

          Administrative agencies have only those powers expressly conferred and those necessary

to accomplish their duties . State v. Jackson, 316 S . W. 2d 341 , 344 (Tex . 1964 ); Sexton v. Mount

Olivet Cemetery Ass 'n, 110 S . W. 2d 129 , 137 (Tex . App .-Austin 1986 , writ ref' d n . r. e .). The

Legislature of Texas sets policy through the enactment of laws and the Commission, as a creature

of statute, is tasked with implementing those laws. Here, the Commission has approved a Plan that

appears to reach beyond the Legislature's clear direction. The Legislature must be afforded the

time to review the Plan and its potential impacts so it can then enact additional legislation to

provide whatever additional guidance it deems fit. As the Legislature is already endeavoring to

tackle the growth in electric demand spurred by data centers popping up across the state, now is

the ideal time for the Legislature to review the Plan as part of a holistic review of the state's

reliability efforts.

          As a state agency, the Commission must operate within the bounds of its enabling statutes.

The Legislature directed the Commission to develop a plan, not to implement it in the manner it

plans. When one is granted an apple, he does not acquire the whole tree. That is even more true

here when that Plan contemplates the use of 765 KV transmission lines which do not appear to

have been contemplated by the legislature. A statute grants an agency exclusive jurisdiction when

its "language clearly expresses the Legislature's intent for the [agencyl to have exclusive

jurisdiction over matters the [statutel governs." Subaru qfAmerica, Inc., v. DavidMcDavidNissan,

84 S.W.3d 212, 223 (Tex. 2002). The Legislature has given an agency exclusive jurisdiction over

a matter when the statute either (1) contains express language to that effect; or (2) creates "a

pervasive regulatory scheme indicat[ingl that the Legislature intended for the regulatory process

to be the exclusive means of remedying the problem " at hand . Oncor Electric Delivery Company

 LLC v. Chaparral EnergM LLC, 546 S.W.3d 133, 138 (Tex. 2018) (quoting In re Sw. Bell *l. Co.,

235 S.W.3d 619, 624-625 (Tex. 2007)). Of course, "[iln deciding whether a 'pervasive regulatory

scheme' exists, the statutory language is determinative." Id. (citing In re Entergy, 142 S.W.3d 316,

322-323 (Tex. 2004)). PURA Sections 11.002, 11.008, 14.001, and 31.001(a) all indicate the

Legislature's creation of a pervasive regulatory scheme. See id at 138. Tex. Util. Code §§ 11.002

(establishing a comprehensive and adequate regulatory system for public utilities); 11.008

(allowing liberal construction of PURA to promote effectiveness and efficiency of the regulation

of public utilities); 14.001 (authorizing the Commission the general power to regulate and

supervise the business of each public utility within its jurisdiction, including anything specifically

designated or implied by PURA); 3 1.001(a) (protecting and ensuring public interest and protection

in rates and services of electrical utilities). PURA Sections 39.166 and 39.167 are also part of that

regulatory scheme and indicate the Legislature required the Commission to create a Plan. Tex. Util.

Code § 39.166; and Act of May 28, 2023, 88th Leg., R.S., ch. 892, 2023 Tex. Gen. Laws 2640.

While the Commission has been given exclusive jurisdiction and authority to formulate a Plan, it

is less clear the Legislature intended or authorized the Commission to construct a network of

765KV transmission lines.

   a. H.B. 5066 does not expressly authorize incorporating KV765 lines into the Plan.

   In interpreting sections 39.166 and 39.167, a court would consider the entire legislative

structure and context to reflect the legislature's intent. Rodriquez v. Waak, 562 S.W.3d 570,576

(Tex. App.-Houston [lst Dist.] 2018), aff'd, 603 S.W.3d 103 (Tex. 2020). "When construing a

statute, [thel primary objective is to determine the Legislature's intent which, when possible, we

discern from the plain meaning of the words chosen ." In re Estate of Nash, 110 S . W. 3d 914 , 917

(Tex. 2007); see also Tex. Gov't Code § 312.005.

     Both sections mandate the Commission to develop a reliability plan to implement, but nowhere

in the plain language of the statute are 765KV lines mentioned. Without that express mandate, the

Commission should pause to allow the Legislature time to evaluate the benefits and risks of these

massive transmission lines. While the potential benefit of such lines may be significant, so is the

risk of damage to privately owned lands and natural resources and the Legislature has not yet had

the ability to balance those interests.

         Neither H.B. 5066 as Introduced nor as Enrolled contains language that would lend

credence to the Commission's interpretation that 765KV lines should be included as part of the

statutorily directed Plan. In fact, the specific language provides for the Plan to:

         (1) address extending transmission services where mineral resources have been found

         (2) address increasing available capacity to meet forecasted load; and

         (3) provide available infrastructure to reduce interconnection times in areas without access

         to transmission service.

Act of May 28, 2023, 88th Leg., R.S., ch. 892, 2023 Tex. Gen. Laws 2640 (codified at Tex. Util.

Code §§ 37.056, 37.0561, and 39.167(expired Sept. 1, 2025)). In the Commission's Order

approving the Plan, the Commission approved at least three 765KV lines, going further than

addressing localized need as it further plans to build the lines on a "statewide basis." Order 55718.

Public sentiment is loud and clear; the public strongly opposes the Plan and its massive reach. The

purpose and spirit of H . B . 5066 is limited to improving and creating regional frameworks . And ,

before the Commission uses that authority to revamp the state 's transmission network , the

Legislature must be allowed to review the potential impacts of a decision as monumental as adding

765KV lines and provide its guidance on whether and how to implement such a change.

    b.   The Fiscal Note does not rellect the Commission's expansive implementation.




                                               Page 6
    The Legislative Budget Board (LBB) must include in its fiscal note for a bill any provision that

would authorize or require expenditures outside of the General Appropriations Act. Tex. Govt

Code § 314.001. LBB must include a cost estimate for a five-year period that begins on the

effective date of the bill and must state whether costs or diversions will be involved after that

period. Id § 3 14.002. LBB included no additional anticipated costs to the state or consumers in its

five-year forecast. Fiscal Note, H.B. 5066, 88#1 Leg., R.S. (2023). A comparison to another fiscal

note from the same session is instructive. S.B. 2012 (88R), as Introduced, had a fiscal note that

noted the bill would require transmission and distiibution to build out generation capacity and that

such costs would be recovered in the utility rates. Fiscal Note, S.B. 2012, 88#1 Leg., R.S. (2023).

Clearly, when LBB anticipated future costs for building electric utility infrastructure during the

88th Session, it noted that there would be a cost and how the cost would be recovered. No such

language was included for H.B. 5066.

   In addition, a Fiscal Note must be attached to the bill for the remainder of its lifespan, including

as part of committee reports and all subsequent printings, including when it is submitted to the

Governor. Tex. Govt Code § 314.003. As previously established, LBB noted no anticipated cost

for this bill, even costs that would be recovered through utility rates. This means that neither the

members who reviewed the bill, nor the committees that considered the bill, nor any member who

voted to approve the bill, nor the Governor, had any notice of the immense costs that the Plan as

currently envisioned by PUC would incur.

   Under the Plan, the Commission is attempting to approve and build lines across the entire state

in an extraordinary change and increase of expense to the citizens of Texas without clear

Legislative direction. These costs should not be borne by the public unless such costs have been

clearly authorized by the Legislature. The Legislature should be allowed to review the proposed




                                              Page 7
 Plan's costs and the fiscal impact to the state so that it can make an informed policy decision.

While the Legislature has begun to review the impact of data centers across the state, it should be

allowed to formulate the state's overall policy going forward considering the enormous costs of

PUC's proposed Plan.

industrial sector, including where heavy oil and gas development are located. State Affairs

Committee Report (Substituted), Bill Analysis, Tex. C.S.H.B. 5066,88th R.S. (2023).

deadline for the Commission to approve or deny an application to the 180th day after the filing

date.1 Nowhere in any version of the bill are 765KV lines mentioned, and the Legislature had

    IV.      Testimony on Floor foreshadowing of what could happen has happened

    The House Committee on State Affairs, in addition to hearing live testimony on H.B. 5066, at

the same hearing also heard testimony on H.B. 4831.2 A representative from both the Commission

and ERCOT appeared as resource witnesses. Representative Raymond wanted clarification on

what the assessments would include under the bill, to which the Commission responded that once

the details of the finalized plan are worked out, and once they get input from the Legislature, that

cost, and cost estimates are something that needs to be addressed. 5:00:47. In further clarification

to the representative, the Commission again stated that cost impact is something that has to be

addressed [by the Legislaturel. 5:01:33.

    Testimony for H.B. 4831 clearly demonstrates that the Commission is aware that the

Legislature defines its limits through "guardrails" and the Legislature must provide it with the

"guardrails" because these are matters of policy. 5:03:27. Testimony from the Commission makes

clear that even the Commission understands there are limits to be observed, especially in the face

of policy questions. It is striking that, in contrast, for H.B. 5066, the Commission does not seek

guardrails or further policy instruction from the Legislature.

    V.       Conclusion

    The Commission should defer to the Legislature and abate any decisions regarding further

development, implementation, or approval of any transmission lines under the Plan. The

Legislature, as the policy-making body of this state, must have the opportunity to review the Plan
